content.p: On 13 May 2005, troops and armoured vehicles fired into a crowd in Bobur Square, in the eastern Uzbek city of Andijan. The government said armed Islamic extremists had caused the deaths. Human Rights Watch, which interviewed more than 50 witnesses and victims in Andijan and in Kyrgyzstan, concluded that the killings were a massacre by government forces. Twenty years later the official figure is still 187, rights groups put the toll far higher, and Tashkent has refused calls for an independent international inquiry.
content.h2: The trial and the prison break
content.p: The crowd had gathered over a trial. Twenty-three Andijan businessmen were on trial over alleged membership of a banned religious group, Akramiya, and many local people believed the case was unfair. Human Rights Watch reported that hundreds of people had protested peacefully against the trial in the weeks before 13 May. The Norwegian Helsinki Committee and two partner groups described the same 23 entrepreneurs as on trial for extremism over alleged membership of Akramiya.

On the day itself, armed men seized weapons from a military barracks and a police station, freed the businessmen from prison and took officials hostage in the regional government building. Human Rights Watch was clear that these men committed serious crimes under Uzbek law. Human Rights Watch accepted that the state could stop the hostage-taking, but said that this did not justify shooting unarmed people on a mass scale.

Later in the day the protest grew into a rally of thousands in the square. Witnesses told Human Rights Watch that the protesters' grievances were overwhelmingly about poverty, corruption and repression, and it found no evidence that any of the speakers promoted an Islamist agenda. The government's version differed. President Islam Karimov said that the gunmen had used people as human shields and that the organisers were fanatics who wanted an Islamic state.

The shooting, according to Human Rights Watch, was not limited to one moment. Witnesses described troops on armoured personnel carriers and military trucks, and snipers, firing into crowds that were mostly unarmed. In all but one incident that witnesses described, no warning was given and no other crowd-control method was tried. After troops sealed off the area around the square, they kept firing as people tried to flee. Human Rights Watch said that one group of fleeing protesters, numbering up to 400, was almost entirely killed by gunfire, and that only a handful of them survived. Human Rights Watch said the presence of armed men did not justify that outcome.

Journalists were also affected. Human Rights Watch reported that Uzbek authorities made some reporters in Andijan leave, seized their materials; other journalists were effectively prevented from entering the city afterwards.

The government's 2005 account gave 173 dead, and later official figures gave 187. In its 2005 account the government counted law enforcement officers and civilians killed by the attackers, along with the attackers themselves. Fergana, summarising the official version on the 20th anniversary, said that 12 law enforcement officers were killed, that 334 weapons were seized, and that 70 people were taken hostage, 15 of whom were later killed.

Human Rights Watch did not give a single number. It said that the government's sealing off of the city made the true toll very hard to establish, that witnesses had been warned by local officials not to talk, and that it believed hundreds had been killed. Eyewitnesses told the group that between 300 and 400 people were present at the worst shooting incident. Human Rights Watch said that the figure given by the government was far lower than eyewitness accounts suggested.

The Norwegian Helsinki Committee, with two partner groups, said in May 2025 that the events had killed hundreds of civilians and that official figures put the number at 187, while refugees from Andijan believed the figure was much higher. Fergana reported that human rights groups now estimate between 500 and 1,500 dead. These estimates were made by different groups, and none of them has been confirmed by an official inquiry. The reports do not agree on a single figure.
content.h2: Bodies, silence and the search for graves
content.p: Many families found their relatives' bodies in the streets or in the local morgue. Human Rights Watch noted that it was not clear where most of the bodies were taken. It said it could not verify persistent rumours of mass graves outside the city, but that a large number of bodies clearly did not end up in the morgue.

The silence has lasted. The 2025 statement said the authorities still refused to verify reports of mass graves linked to the events, and had taken no transparent steps to clarify what happened. The same statement noted that a business centre was planned for Bobur Square, where the violence took place, and called that an apparent attempt to avoid confronting the past.
content.h2: Sanctions and the refusal of an inquiry
content.p: The international response was sharp at first. Human Rights Watch told Washington to stop negotiating over a long-term American military presence in Uzbekistan, and asked the European Union to suspend its Partnership and Cooperation Agreement until Tashkent allowed an independent international inquiry. The Uzbek government rejected such an inquiry as unnecessary. Its foreign minister said foreign diplomats would be allowed to monitor an investigation by the Uzbek parliament, which Human Rights Watch said would utterly lack credibility.

The European Union responded with visa bans on 12 Uzbek officials, an arms embargo and a partial suspension of its cooperation agreement. In November 2006, RFE/RL reported that the council had extended the visa restrictions on the 12 officials for another six months, and had decided to resume "technical meetings" with the Uzbek leadership. Pierre Morel, the special representative for Central Asia, told RFE/RL that the decision aimed at "adapting" the sanctions regime. The Norwegian Helsinki Committee and Fergana both say the sanctions remained until 2009. The United States closed its Khanabad base, according to the Norwegian Helsinki Committee.

In 2013, members of the Uzbek government delegation declared at a UN human rights review that Andijan was a closed issue, according to Fergana. The 2025 statement said that Uzbekistan had continued to refuse calls for an independent international investigation.

Thousands of people fled Andijan, and many crossed into Kyrgyzstan. Human Rights Watch reported that Uzbek security services pressured the relatives of refugees who were in Kyrgyzstan, including an elderly man who travelled to a refugee camp to persuade his own relatives to come home.

Five men were handed over to Uzbekistan from Osh on 9 August 2006. RFE/RL reported that four of them had been arrested in June 2005 and held despite the UN refugee agency's acknowledgement that they were asylum seekers. The UN refugee agency's representative in Kyrgyzstan, Vitaly Maslovsky, called the decision "very wrong" because it contravened the 1951 UN convention on refugees. Human rights groups had urged Bishkek not to send the men back, warning that they could face torture or execution.

The European Court of Human Rights gave a further ruling in April 2008 in Ismoilov v. Russia. The court barred Russia from extraditing a group of Uzbek refugees to Uzbekistan, where they feared torture. Human Rights Watch, which filed a brief in the case, said the judgment rejected Uzbekistan's diplomatic assurances against torture as unreliable and insufficient.
content.h2: Prosecutions, the crackdown and later admissions
content.p: Human Rights Watch reported that the Uzbek government had cast nearly all its domestic critics as terrorists and extremists for years. The Norwegian Helsinki Committee said that in the years after May 2005 hundreds of witnesses were reportedly arrested for questioning, and that several hundred human rights activists, journalists and opponents were imprisoned on what the groups called trumped-up charges. It also reported that civil society activists and political exiles were reportedly listed by the security services alongside terrorists, and that most of those who fled had been stripped of their citizenship and had not been able to regain it.

Former residents of Andijan have been convicted for taking part in the 2005 protests as recently as 2023. The Norwegian Helsinki Committee cited the case of Kayumov Mukhamadvali, who was sentenced to more than 15 years in prison on 5 January 2023 after returning from Sweden, where he had lived for 18 years.

Official statements have also changed in tone. In 2019, the former interior minister Zokir Almatov, who had been involved in the events, told the Qalampir.uz website that the violence was a response to an attempted coup, and said, "Sorry, but we did everything we could at the time." In February 2020, Deputy Prosecutor General Svetlana Artykova told the same site that civilians were among the victims, and attributed the deaths to poor coordination between troops and their commanders. She also said that those responsible for shooting civilians had been prosecuted and that some had already served their sentences. Fergana noted that the Qalampir interview is no longer available online.

When President Shavkat Mirziyoyev came to power in December 2016, he ordered the release of dozens of imprisoned activists and journalists, and promised reforms to address past injustices. Fergana described a period of relative thaw, in which some media dared to mention Andijan. The Norwegian Helsinki Committee said that backsliding on rights had since set in, and that witnesses remain afraid to speak.

The official figure of 187 dead has not been revised by an independent inquiry, and the government has not allowed one. The Andijan events are therefore still disputed. The official account blames armed Islamic extremists, while rights groups and witnesses say that troops killed hundreds of unarmed civilians. The 2025 statement from the Norwegian Helsinki Committee and two partner groups says that the people responsible have not been brought to justice.
